title: Bo: a sign upon your hand (Exodus 13:9, 16)
hookLine: the Exodus is remembered on the hand and between the eyes, a root of tefillin

lines: A RING. A STRING. A WATCH.
cards: A wedding ring. A string on a wrist from a grandmother. A watch that belonged to someone who's gone.
A medical bracelet. Some things people remember in their heads, and some on their skin, where their hands brush them again and again without trying. Bo is ending.
The plagues are over, the night of the Exodus has come and gone, and the people are finally out. And the portion's last word on the matter isn't a story or a song. It's a sign, worn on the body.

teach.b: Twice, near the end of Bo, the Torah says the Exodus should be remembered on the body. The first time: "And it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thy hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes."
A few verses later, it's for a sign upon thy hand, and for frontlets between thine eyes.

Jewish tradition reads these verses, and two more in Deuteronomy, as the command of tefillin: two small black leather boxes, one bound on the arm, by tradition facing the heart, one on the head above the forehead, worn in weekday morning prayer.
Inside the boxes are four handwritten passages from the Torah. Two are from this very portion, the two you just heard. The other two are from Deuteronomy, the Shema and the paragraph after it.
So on weekday mornings the Exodus is literally bound on the arm.

The word for frontlets, totafot, is a puzzle; nobody is certain where it comes from. The Talmud plays with it as two foreign words that each mean two, which add up to the four compartments of the head box.
Whatever its origin, the idea is plain: memory that lives only in your head fades.
Memory bound to your hand and your eyes stays where you'll keep bumping into it.
And with that, Bo is done: come, not go; the darkness; the new moon; the telling; and the sign on the hand.

how: Jews who keep the practice, traditionally men and in some communities women too, put on tefillin for weekday morning prayer, binding one box on the arm and one on the head; tefillin are not worn on Shabbat or festivals.

games.q: the Exodus is over. how does the end of Bo say it should be remembered?
o: a yearly speech in the town square.
a sign upon the hand and between the eyes.
a monument at the border of Egypt.
games.why: twice, on the hand and between the eyes. tradition reads it as tefillin, with these very verses inside.

practice: Rest one hand on your other forearm and feel the weight of it. Is there anything you wear that carries a memory, a ring, a bracelet, a scar you've made peace with, a shirt someone gave you?
If there is, touch it and let the memory come; if not, choose something now, a hair tie, a watch on the other wrist, and give it a job: to remind you of one thing you've been freed from.
